idiom_name: gorilla/sessions Store/Session with stdlib crypto/rand and net/http cookie
implementation_notes: The standard library supplies primitives but no store: crypto/rand for identifiers and net/http Cookie with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite for transport. gorilla/sessions supplies the classic roles as a Store interface plus a per-request Session with Values, Options and Save; cookie stores sign (and optionally encrypt) the payload, while Redis- or database-backed stores keep an opaque identifier server-side. The manager collapses into the store implementation plus the request-scoped session accessor; what remains hand-written is policy: regenerate the identifier on login, invalidate on logout, set Options with max age, HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite.
code_sketch:
var store = sessions.NewCookieStore(key)          // or a redis-backed sessions.Store
s, _ := store.Get(r, "sid")                       // identifier validated by the store
s.Values["user"] = user.ID
s.Options = &sessions.Options{Path: "/", HttpOnly: true, Secure: true,
    SameSite: http.SameSiteStrictMode, MaxAge: 1800}
_ = s.Save(r, w)                                  // logout: MaxAge: -1, clear values
pitfalls: CookieStore signs but does not encrypt, so session values are readable by the client; keep only an opaque reference or enable encryption.
The in-process MemoryStore loses every session on restart and does not work across instances; it is a development default, not a deployment choice.
Forgetting Save leaves the identifier only in the handler: the browser never receives the cookie and the next request starts a fresh session.
A store read per request on a hot path can dominate latency; keep the store local or cached and read the session conditionally.
